POD-MOUTH.notes: THIS SUPERSEDES TWO EARLIER DESCRIPTIONS, and the accepted glimpse still shows the second of them. The first put two web banks flanking a central aisle with the viewport on the far bulkhead. The second, which the accepted DR-108_TURN-270_POD-DOOR-OPEN_V2_R4 was painted to on 2026-09-16, moved the web to one side but left THE CONSOLE ON THE NORTH SIDE WALL. DR-112 moved the console from the north wall to the BACK (WEST) BULKHEAD the same day -- scripts/fabric-feinstein.mjs says so in as many words -- because the user asked for "the control panel against the back wall" and because the north wall had to be cleared for a porthole worth looking through. So R4 now shows lamps on the right-hand wall where the porthole belongs, and a bare far bulkhead where the console belongs. IT IS LEFT AND RIGHT CORRECT AND FRONT WRONG, which is the easiest kind of error to miss. The glimpse must be re-edited.

TURN-000.reason: The porthole square on, and the view that caught dev's camera error. R1 showed the pane running edge to edge with no rim and no jambs, which a 2.4 m pane 1.15 m from the eye CANNOT do -- it subtends about 92 degrees of a 110 degree lens, so there must be cabin wall down both sides. There is: the fluted wall runs down the far left and the far right, the pane sits between them with its top rim and the hull above it, and the vault ribs come down into frame. The pane is black here because that is the DOCKED-DARK state -- the pod is still in its ejection tube and the bore is a hand's breadth beyond the glass. LANDED, RISING and SUBMERGED change what is behind it. check-seed PASS at 0.00 invented, 1.02 dropped.

The state the player meets first and looks at longest: I-POD-TRIP puts both in the room on the same turn, so this holds from the thud until one is taken. It carries two leaf conditions where the single-object variants carry one, so turn.js ranks it above both and hands over to them as each object is picked up. R3, 2026-09-21, at the user's instruction with a screenshot: the kit and the towel are about 3x their canon size and stand ON THE OPEN DECK clear of the safety webbing, where the earlier art had them in a recess inside the web bay. fabric-feinstein.mjs fills z 0.0 to 1.50 with the web mass (WEB_NEAR, WEB_BACK), so the deck is the 1.55 m strip against the north hull, and that is where they are. The towel's lettering is canon verbatim -- "S.P.S. FEINSTEIN / Escape Pod #42 / Don't Panic!" (globals.zil 1002-1005). Composited over the accepted seed, not re-rendered: 146252 px changed, every one inside x691-1258 y486-939, and the three siblings differ from each other in ZERO of the 1,315,480 pixels outside that box. R2 was sent back for exactly that -- it re-rendered the whole frame (394,362 to 448,661 px, box the full 1672x941), moving the ceiling by 17.7% and the webbing by 20.7%, so picking up the towel would have shifted the room.

notes: DR-112 REBUILD (the user, 2026-09-16, after playing the opening sequence). The room is re-cut and every earlier painted view is superseded -- see supersededImages. What the room is now, in the user's own words as you meet it from Deck Nine: WEBBING ON THE LEFT ONLY, THE CONTROL PANEL ON THE BACK BULKHEAD, A LARGE PORTHOLE ON THE RIGHT ONLY. Left is south, right is north, back is west.

The webbing is ONE mass filling the south half, near strap plane z 0.0 and back curtain on the hull at 1.50 -- half the pod, which is what canon says ("a mass of safety webbing ... fills half the pod", globals.zil 1084-1092). The porthole is 2.4 x 1.1 centred 1.25 m up on the north flank, in a 0.18 m well let into the vault's curved flank: a well and not a hole, because a flat pane cannot lie in a curved hull. The console stands on the west bulkhead with its lamp row, and the service column at the back-south corner holds the supply compartment, open from TRIP-COUNTER 15.

THIS ROOM'S EYE STANDS, 1.6 m, backed hard against the webbing (0.30 m clear of the near strap plane) and 1.25 m off the porthole. It is not at the middle of the box: the middle is inside the webbing now. At the strip's centre the enlarged pane filled the frame as a blank slab with no rim in sight, which is why it is backed up. The scene file is cut about this eye.

WHAT THIS EYE PAINTS, and what it does not. The player is strapped into the webbing from the explosion to the thud (DR-112, rules/ship.js), so the whole descent -- the Feinstein blowing apart, the planet growing from four thousand miles to the surf -- is seen from ESCAPE-POD-WEB and NOT from here. This eye paints the window black in the tube before the launch, and then landed, water rising and submerged, which is what you see when you stand up and escape. Anything else through this porthole is the other room's.

Three deviations from Infocom's text stand behind those states, all the user's decisions of 2026-09-16 and all already in the rules (rules/ship.js, pinned by scripts/tests/pod.mjs): the viewport no longer polarizes black, so the descent is visible where the source blacked it out; the web will not let you out between the explosion and the thud, so the source's landing death is unreachable; and standing is implicit, so the escape after the thud is a turn shorter and a LOOK no longer drowns you.

The pod as built (DR-109-GEOMETRY-DEV-ANSWER.md, approved by the user 14 Sep; fabric wwwroot/data/scenes/ESCAPE-POD.json from scripts/fabric-feinstein.mjs): a 4.0 m cabin level with Deck Nine's deck under a ribbed barrel vault (floor chord 2.4, crown 2.4, widest 3.0 m at 0.9 m), to the floor plan of Deck Nine's accepted TURN-270 POD-DOOR-OPEN glimpse. Pod = Deck Nine + [5.6, 0, 0]; `size` is the vault's envelope.

One eye, on the aisle 2.0 m in from the door. One door: the east bulkhead is Deck Nine's west wall and the leaf is Deck Nine's own; EAST, OUT and UP are that one mouth. Four ribs at the web columns (0.79, 1.55, 2.38, 3.08 m in). The far (west) bulkhead carries the console with its lamp row under the viewport, and south of it the service column whose flush supply compartment (x -1.7, y 0.9-1.4, z 0.7-1.2) cannot be told from the column until it opens.
No invented lettering (no ESCAPE POD 42, PROVISIONS or CAPACITY), no occupant number, no lasting tilt, no warm accent; FOOD-KIT and TOWEL are runtime assets, never painted.

Norm plan (DR-109, 14 Sep): TURN-000/090/180/270, pitch 0, HFOV 110, 1672x941; caps UP/DOWN pitch +90/-90, HFOV 131, 1254 square, all from the eye [0, 1.6, 0]. Seam windows are 43-47, 133-137, 223-227 and 313-317 degrees (spans 90, each under 94), all on the web banks' inner faces between columns; each window is 6.1 degrees or more from the arch where the vault meets an end bulkhead (53.1, 126.9, 233.1, 306.9), 7.8 from the service column (234.8) and 20.7 from an opening. Each opening is whole inside one view: the door (67.7-112.3) in 090, the viewport (255.6-284.4) in 270, with the console (247.9-292.1), the service column and the compartment (234.8-247.6). States: TURN-270 owns the viewport group (base DOCKED; @DEBRIS, @BLACK, @OCEAN, @ISLAND, @LANDED, @RISING, @SUBMERGED); TURN-090 and TURN-DOWN own the door (base DOOR-SHUT; @OPEN-DOCKED, @OPEN-FLOOD). The DOWN cap reaches 0.71 m up the door plane and 0.83 m up the service column, under the compartment's 0.9 m sill, so it has no compartment variant; UP sees neither opening. Fabric renders in reference/DR-109_ESCAPE-POD-*_FABRIC*.png. Seeds 270 and 090 first.

JOIN WARNINGS, ANSWERED AND NOT TO BE RE-OPENED (16 Sep). review-room reports three straight lines lying along joins: level-045 at TURN-000's top edge, and up-135 and up-225 at TURN-180's -- the last two being one line seen from both diagonals, not two faults. All three are the vault's CROWN RIBS and the pipe beside the lamp, which the fabric carries (DR-109_ESCAPE-POD-180_FABRIC-V2.png shows them arcing over the vault at just those angles). They are the room's own structure lying on the join, so they are notes, not paint that stops on a boundary, and they must NOT be seam-edited: seam would ramp a real rib out. Greg looked at all three at original size (20260916-180221-design-0205) and dev checked the claim against the fabric rather than taking it. Why the tool still calls them warnings rather than notes: it decides that by reading the guide's own full-frame blockout beside the join, and these joins have none registered (the caps), so it cannot tell and says so the cautious way. Expect them on every future run of this room.

THE `eye` FIELD IS IN SCENE COORDINATES, NOT ROOM COORDINATES, AND MUST STAY [0, 1.6, 0]. DO NOT "CORRECT" IT TO z -0.30. Dev did exactly that on 2026-09-17, reasoning that scripts/fabric-feinstein.mjs carries ROOMS[ESCAPE-POD].eye = [-5.6, 0, -0.30] while this file said z 0, and that the two disagreed. They do not. The fabric writer SHIFTS every part by that eye when it writes the scene -- wwwroot/data/scenes/ESCAPE-POD.json has the porthole at z -1.15, which is the room-coordinate -1.45 plus 0.30 -- so the scene file already has the eye at its origin. wwwroot/scene/graybox.js then places the camera AT `eye` inside that shifted scene, so z 0 is the standing position in the open strip and z -0.30 puts the camera 0.30 m FURTHER north, 0.85 m off a 2.4 m pane instead of 1.15 m. The cost was not subtle: every one of the six blockouts moved between 47% and 81% of the frame, TURN-000 lost both side jambs and the pane ran edge to edge, and a seed pair was painted from the wrong camera before a render was looked at. THE PACKAGE MIXES TWO FRAMES ON PURPOSE AND EACH FIELD SAYS WHICH: `eye` is scene coordinates (eye at the origin), while `size`, `wallOpenings`, `exits`, `largeObjects` and `droppedItems` are ROOM coordinates, which is why the porthole reads z -1.45 here. The sister package ESCAPE-POD-WEB follows the same rule -- its eye is [0, 1.2, 0] and its porthole reads z -2.65, being 1.45 + 1.20 from the seated eye. ONE KNOWN WRINKLE, LEFT ALONE DELIBERATELY: scripts/check_design.mjs measures the dropped-item lanes and the proxy sight lines from `eye` against room-coordinate positions, so for this room those tests run from a point 0.30 m off. That is a 0.30 m error in a clearance test with a 0.5 m bar, and it is worth less than breaking every view of the room. Fix it in the checker if it is ever worth fixing; do not fix it here.

THE RING IS 000 / 090 / 180 / 270 AT 110 DEGREES, WITH UP AND DOWN CAPS AT 131, and it hangs: neighbours are 90 degrees apart, inside the 94-degree limit that turn.js solveSeams imposes (at a 90-degree span its window is lo = max(8, 90-47) = 43 to hi = min(90-8, 47) = 47, which is not empty). The ring is aligned to the walls rather than offset from them because this room is read from its door: TURN-270 is the establishing view, square down the long axis with the webbing left, the console ahead and the porthole right, and the other three are the walls either side of it.

IN-WEB IS WITHDRAWN AS A STATE OF THIS ROOM (2026-09-17) AND MUST NOT COME BACK. It hung on "ADVENTURER in SAFETY-WEB" and was meant to show the player up in the webbing, seen from the floor. That condition is now the one that routes the view to ESCAPE-POD-WEB instead: while it holds, the game renders the nest and never this room, so a variant hung on it can never be reached. It is also a picture of something impossible -- you cannot stand on the floor and be in the web at the same time. Its condition was "ADVENTURER in SAFETY-WEB". If the routing is ever removed, this becomes paintable again and not before.

OPEN-FLOOD IS WITHDRAWN (2026-09-17) FOR TWO REASONS, EITHER OF WHICH WOULD BE ENOUGH. FIRST, IT COULD NEVER HAVE HUNG: its condition was "POD-DOOR has OPENBIT and TRIP-COUNTER >= 15", character for character the same as FLOOR-WATER’s, and two variants on one condition mean one of them is never chosen. SECOND, WHAT IT SHOWS CANNOT HAPPEN: it paints the door open on rock and sea with the floor still dry, and the change is confined to the doorway -- the grating is the seed’s own pixels. There is no such turn. Played through from the landing: standing takes SINK-COUNTER to 1 and queues I-SINK-POD, opening the door takes it to 2, and the opening itself says "The bulkhead opens and cold ocean water rushes in!". The door is never open on the sea before the water is in. FLOOR-WATER, which paints the same doorway with water across the grating, is the true picture of that condition and is the one registered. THE GENERAL SHAPE OF THIS MISTAKE IS WORTH KEEPING: a state list can name a beat the prose implies but the clocks never hold open, and neither check-seed nor check-state can see it, because both ask whether a painting matches the geometry, not whether the game can ever reach it. Play it.

THE PROVISIONS PANEL NEEDS THREE VARIANTS, NOT TWO, AND THE THIRD IS THE ONE THE PLAYER SEES FIRST. FOOD-KIT-PRESENT and TOWEL-PRESENT hang on "sceneObjects contains FOOD-KIT" and "... contains TOWEL", one leaf condition each. But I-POD-TRIP moves BOTH objects into the room on the same turn, so from the landing until something is taken both conditions hold at once -- and turn.js picks by specificity, sorting variants by leaf count and taking the first that holds (dashboard/turn.js, foldVariants and pickVariants). Two variants of equal depth means one of them wins arbitrarily, and the panel shows a kit and no towel, or a towel and no kit, in the very state where both are sitting in it. PROVISIONS-BOTH carries two leaf conditions, so it outranks both and is chosen while both objects are present; each single-object variant then takes over when the other has been picked up. The same rule is why a base view never competes with its own variants. This was found by reading what the rules do on the turn the panel opens, not by any checker: like IN-WEB and OPEN-FLOOD before it, the fault is in WHICH states exist rather than in any picture, and no tool that compares a painting to geometry can see it.

SIBLING STATES MUST AGREE ON EVERYTHING THEY BOTH SHOW, and the way to check that is to compare them with EACH OTHER, not only with the base. check-state compares a variant against the view it departs from, and by that test all three provisions variants were perfect -- every changed pixel inside the panel rectangle and exactly zero outside it. It cannot see that two variants disagree about the thing they are both departures of. Here the cabinet itself was drawn differently in TOWEL-PRESENT, so the panel would change shape as its contents were removed, and the tell was arithmetic before it was visual: BOTH differs from the kit by 12,708 px, which is about what adding a towel costs, but from the towel by 31,986. When one of three siblings is several times further from the others, the odd one out is usually redrawing something it should have inherited.

DR-112 IS COMPLETE (2026-09-17). The escape pod is two packages and they are both finished. ESCAPE-POD-WEB, the seat inside the safety web, carries one master frame and fifteen state variants -- the whole launch and descent, from the pane black against the tube bore to the sea closing over it. ESCAPE-POD, the eye standing on the floor, carries a ring of four at 110 degrees with UP and DOWN caps at 131, and eleven state variants. DECK-NINE’s glimpse through the open bulkhead agrees with ESCAPE-POD’s own TURN-270. Every state the game can reach has a picture, and three that it cannot were found and withdrawn: IN-WEB, which the art-room routing made unreachable; OPEN-FLOOD, whose condition duplicated FLOOR-WATER’s and whose dry floor no turn holds open; and R1 of TOWEL-PRESENT, which disagreed with its siblings about the cabinet.

SAFETY-WEB.notes: The south web bank; the north bank has no pick proxy, since an object takes one position and size. The two banks are charcoal strap-ladder webbing in a frame, 0.75 to 3.15 m in from the door, clipped by the vault (Greg, 20260914-013234-design-0029). Boarding it moves the player, not the web. IT IS A LARGE OBJECT, NOT A THING STANDING IN THE ROOM (the user, 2026-09-16: "when adventurer in safety web is unchecked, the wall shows up as a big blue block"). The web is in every approved view -- the nets ARE the painting -- so drawing it as well put a 2.4 x 2.2 m steel-blue placeholder (graybox.js COLORS.vehicle, because SAFETY-WEB carries VEHBIT) across the bank. Here it is carried through with `painted`, like the ladder across the rift, and is a pick target only.

supersededImages.note: Every view registered before DR-112, kept for the record. The user asked on 2026-09-16 to 'scrap what weve got on the escape pod': the room they are of no longer exists. Do not hang them and do not build from them. OPEN-FLOOD, withdrawn 2026-09-17: kept on disk and named here so nobody paints it again.

notes: THE DATUM. Heights are shared with the Crag and the Balcony (CRAG.json note): day-one sea level is the datum, the Crag's floor is 2 m above it, the Balcony's floor 8 m above the Crag's. In THIS room's coordinates the seabed is the floor at y 0, the eye 1.6 above it, and the day-one sea surface is at y 16.2 -- so the player on the bottom floats 14.6 m under the surface, and the Crag's floor is at y 18.2, its cleft lip the 2 m of rock between the water and it. The user's decision of 2026-09-18 (DR-115): the water was 4.6 m deep (surface at y 6.2) until then, and at that depth the climb's three stages rose 1.4 m each and the seabed never left the frame. None of the six accepted paintings shows a waterline, so none of them changes; the accepted FABRIC (scenes/UNDERWATER.json) keeps its sea plane at 6.2 so that its views do not move, and the one water column the depths are cut from (scripts/fabric-underwater.mjs) has it at 16.2. The face stands 5.6 m north of the eye, with the loose rocks the player is buffeted against closer in.

THE CLIFF IS NORTH, the open sea south, exactly as at the Crag and the Balcony. This is the same face carrying on below the waterline: the island 'rises from the water' (compone.zil 38-39) on the north side of both rooms, so a player who surfaces at the cleft and climbs out is facing the way they already were.

ONE WATER VOLUME, NOT A BOX. Four of the five exits lead back here (compone.zil 19-22): DOWN, WEST, NORTH and SOUTH all return UNDERWATER, and only UP reaches the Crag. So the room has no far wall to paint in three directions -- south, west and east the water simply fails into nothing, and that failure is the fog, not a surface. The one solid thing in the room is the cliff face to the north and the rocks at its foot.

WHY THERE ARE NO DAY STATES. The player can be here on any day: day 1 out of the pod (POD-EXIT-F, globals.zil 929), and from the Balcony, the Winding Stair or the Courtyard once the flood has taken each of them (ship.js 186-188). But the rising sea is a change in where the surface IS, and from the seabed, at this fog, the surface is a dim brightening overhead in every case. Nothing the eye can tell apart, so one look serves every day and there is no DAY-PHASE here. The Crag, which is dry on day 1 and gone after, carries that change instead.

DROWNING IS NOT DRAWN. Three turns here kills (compone.zil 28-32, ship.js 150-151). The brief is explicit that the clock is not artwork: no vignette, no darkening, no bubbles counting down. The room looks the same on the first turn and the third, and the engine says the rest.

FLOYD can follow the player here (I-FLOYD has no room test, compone.zil 2186-2195), but it is rare: when sceneObjects contains FLOYD, draw the shared placeholder at a fallback anchor clear of the UP route. No authored anchor is required. (DR-003, kept from the 2026-09-11 review.)

NOTHING HERE IS CLICKABLE BUT THE WAY OUT. UNDERWATER carries no GLOBAL objects and no PSEUDO scenery in the source (compone.zil 7-24) -- unlike the Crag, which has CLIFF, OCEAN, STRUCTURE and CLEFT. So the cliff face the player is being thrown against cannot be examined, and the room's only pick targets are its five exits. That is canon and is not to be 'fixed' with invented scenery; it is also part of why the room is frightening, and why the eye has to do the work.

SNELL'S WINDOW -- the law for the caps, and why neither level seed paints the surface. The fabric draws the sea as a flat plane of one colour (parts.js `sea`); that is a blockout convenience and must NOT be read as an instruction to paint a bright plane overhead. Under water the surface is only transparent inside a cone about 49 degrees from vertical. A level view reaches 38.8 degrees of elevation at lens 110 -- outside that cone everywhere -- so at a level gaze the underside of the surface is a mirror reflecting the dark seabed, indistinguishable from dark water. Both accepted seeds paint it that way and they are right. The UP CAP is the opposite case: looking straight up the eye is inside the cone, so the cap SHOULD carry the bright window with its rim, and beyond the rim the mirrored seabed. That is the one place in this room the surface is real, and it is where the way out is unmistakable.

THE CLEFT IS A CHIMNEY, NOT A HOLE. Dev's first fabric cut the cleft open right through to the north to make it read bright, which made it a hole clean through the island with open sea beyond -- wrong, because the island IS north. It is now closed at the back (z -9.4) and open above, so it is a shaft of lit water: a way UP, not a way through. The accepted TURN-000 seed passes check-seed at the same numbers against the corrected fabric, so nothing was repainted for it.

THE CLIMB IS FOUR DEPTHS, AND EACH DEPTH IS ITS OWN EYE (DR-115). UP from the seabed takes three stages and then leaves the water (rules/ship.js roomExits, scripts/tests/underwater.mjs). The source had one UP straight to the Crag and three turns before the undertow; the user asked for the ascent to be watchable, and chose to pay for it by making the CLIMB free of the drowning clock rather than by loosening the clock -- so dithering still kills you on the third idle turn, and rising never does. Leaving the pod starts you at DEPTH 3, on the bottom; falling in off a flooded ledge starts you at DEPTH 1, near the surface. Swimming DOWN goes deeper again, which is the only way back to the pod. THIS ROOM IS DEPTH 3. The other three are ART ROOMS, second eyes on this room as the safety web is on the escape pod: UNDERWATER-D2, -D1 and -D0, in this package, eyes at 6.4, 11.2 and 15.6 m on the same vertical line, selected by scenes/UNDERWATER.json's `altViews` on DEPTH. Each has its own ring, caps and exit positions; game.js takes one only once it is accepted, so until then every depth shows this room's six paintings. A light grade (brighter up, darker down) was tried here first and the user rejected it on 2026-09-18: the change between depths is geometry, the seabed falling away and the face sliding down, not one room relit.

DR-111, the user 2026-09-16: "if we are underwater and we see the bottom of the sea, then we should still see the open escape pod somewhere". THE CANON, checked: the pod never lands in the sinking sequence -- I-SINK-POD (globals.zil 1329) has it smash against underwater rocks at SINK-COUNTER 3 and keep sinking, creak at 4 and kill you at 5. The thud the user remembered is a different and earlier moment: the pod landing ON the Crag at TRIP-COUNTER 11 (globals.zil 1314, "lands with a thud ... precariously balanced"), and then the shock as it topples into the water when the player stands. BUT after the player leaves, I-SINK-POD prints nothing at all -- it is gated on HERE being the pod -- so canon stops tracking it entirely and says nothing about where it ends up. A pod that sinks and THEN settles is not a deviation; it is the next thirty seconds, which the game never describes. The room says where: the player is against an underwater CLIFF and the pod was last seen striking rocks, so it tumbles down the face and comes to rest at its foot, which is the seabed the player is standing on when they get out. A settled pod is also a far better painted still than a descending one. THE CONDITION: SINK-COUNTER >= 3 is the pod submerged, DEPTH == 3 is the bottom. No upper bound -- it is not going anywhere -- and it is visible only at the bottom, which is what gives swimming DOWN a reason once the climb has started. THE DOWN CAP VARIANT IS WITHDRAWN AND MUST NOT COME BACK (2026-09-16). The user reported seeing TWO pods on the sea floor, and they were: the two paintings put the pod in different places. Measured by diffing each variant against its own base and unprojecting the centroid through that view's camera, the level view puts the pod at bearing 162.6 and elevation -7.7, and the cap put it at bearing 146.2 and elevation -50.5 -- sixteen degrees apart in bearing, which no single object can be, and elevations implying distances that differ ninefold. The level view is the right one: at elevation -7.7 with the eye 1.6 m up, the pod lies about 11.8 m off. THE CAP CANNOT SEE IT. A 131-degree cap reaches elevation -24.5 on its axes and -17.9 at its corners, so a thing at -7.7 is outside it altogether. Dev's DR-111 request asked for a cap variant that the geometry forbids, and the only way to satisfy it was to paint a second, nearer pod. Looking down in this state correctly shows bare seabed.

UP.notes: The cleft, the only way out: a groove in the face that starts at y 2 -- just over eye height -- and widens and brightens all the way up toward the surface (y 16.2 since DR-115; the accepted fabric draws its sea plane at 6.2). The face stands 5.6 m out, which is what puts the whole funnel inside the level ring: at lens 110 a level view reaches y 6.1 at that distance, so the player sees it from its foot to well up the shaft without tipping the camera. That is the package's 'the upward escape route is visually obvious' criterion, met by geometry. Costs 35 minutes (the C-MOVE table).

DOWN.notes: Open water over the seabed, south of the eye, going dark. Leads back to UNDERWATER: the player who swims down is put back where they started, one turn nearer drowning.

NORTH.notes: The rocks at the foot of the face -- 'currents buffet you against the sharp rocks of an underwater cliff' (compone.zil 11-12) is this, together with the loose rocks 2.4 to 3.6 m out that stand in the near foreground of every view. Leads back to UNDERWATER: there is nowhere north to go but into the rock. Kept below y 1.7 so it never overlaps the UP cleft, which starts at 1.9: a click low on the face swims you into it, a click up the bright funnel takes you out.

WEST.notes: Open water along the face, west. Leads back to UNDERWATER.

SOUTH.notes: Open water away from the island, south. Leads back to UNDERWATER.

CRAG-CLEFT.beyond: CRAG: a funnel of broken rock narrowing upward to the surface, the water in it bright and moving, and above the surface the collapsed cleft lip 2 m up -- freshly exposed pale rock where it 'collapsed under the weight of the escape pod' (compone.zil 39-40), against the wet dark basalt either side of it. Seen from under the water the lip is refracted, broken by the surface and never sharp. The Balcony, 8 m higher again, is not visible from here at all.
CRAG-CLEFT.notes: Not an architectural opening: a natural cleft, the same one the Crag's WATER-DESCENT looks down. It is a bay in the face rather than a hole through it, which is why it has a recessDepth and no door. Its height covers the whole funnel, from the groove's foot at y 1.2 to y 6.8 just above the surface, because that is the single feature the eye follows upward -- the planner must not treat the underwater part and the lip as two openings.

OPEN-SEA-SOUTH.beyond: UNDERWATER (itself): open water away from the island, the light failing southward into blue-black with no horizon, no seabed edge and nothing to fix a distance by. Whatever is painted here must have no hard edge in it: the moment the player can see where the water stops, the room has a wall it does not have.
OPEN-SEA-SOUTH.notes: An opening onto nothing, recorded so the view planner knows the south is open water and not a surface to paint.

OPEN-SEA-WEST.beyond: UNDERWATER (itself): the cliff's foot running away west along the north side, the rocks at its base going out of sight in the fog within 15 m or so. Same rule as the south -- no hard edge, nothing to measure the distance by.
OPEN-SEA-WEST.notes: The face carries on west toward the Balcony's cliff, 12 m along at the surface (CRAG.json note), but the fog reaches nothing like that far.

OPEN-SEA-EAST.beyond: UNDERWATER (itself): the same as the west, the face running away east. NOT an exit -- east is not in the room's exit table (compone.zil 15-22) and a player who tries it is told they cannot go that way -- but it is open water and must be painted as such, not as a wall.
OPEN-SEA-EAST.notes: Recorded precisely because it is not an exit: without it the planner would have no reason to think the east is open, and the ring would grow a fourth wall the room does not have.

fog.notes: This is the room. Everything the player cannot see is the reason it is frightening, and at 30 m the far water is gone entirely -- which is also what keeps three open sides honest without painting a wall behind them. Authored rather than inherited: UNDERWATER is not a sky room, so it has no fogTone to take, and the sky rule's 12-to-260 m is an order of magnitude too far for water. The colour doubles as the background (scene/lighting.js), so the nothing beyond the fog is the same water and not a black void -- and because it is lit water rather than dark, the open cleft reads as a bright wedge in the dark face. Not the deep: a darker tone was tried and made the face unreadable. `plates: true` because the paintings are in the water too: plates take no scene fog by default (a painting carries its own atmosphere), but this room was reviewed and accepted with its views fogged, and that look is kept.

fill.notes: Green-blue light with no direction in it: under water the light has been scattered so many times that it comes from everywhere at once. Strong, because there is no key and no fixture and this is the only light the room has -- at 0.75 the rock came out very nearly black. The sense of 'above' comes from the surface being a bright plane overhead and from the cleft, not from a key light.

lighting.notes: No sun and no key. UNDERWATER is deliberately not in the shared sky room list: it has no sky, no horizon and no sun disc, and a directional light under this much water is exactly the hard-edged wrong answer. NO GRADE: a per-depth grade on these six paintings (exposure, tint, saturation, lift for DEPTH-3 to DEPTH-0) was tried for the climb and rejected by the user on 2026-09-18, and removed. POD-ON-BOTTOM.notes: DR-111, the user 2026-09-16: "if we are underwater and we see the bottom of the sea, then we should still see the open escape pod somewhere". THE CANON, checked: the pod never lands in the sinking sequence -- I-SINK-POD (globals.zil 1329) has it smash against underwater rocks at SINK-COUNTER 3 and keep sinking, creak at 4 and kill you at 5. The thud the user remembered is a different and earlier moment: the pod landing ON the Crag at TRIP-COUNTER 11 (globals.zil 1314, "lands with a thud ... precariously balanced"), and then the shock as it topples into the water when the player stands. BUT after the player leaves, I-SINK-POD prints nothing at all -- it is gated on HERE being the pod -- so canon stops tracking it entirely and says nothing about where it ends up. A pod that sinks and THEN settles is not a deviation; it is the next thirty seconds, which the game never describes. The room says where: the player is against an underwater CLIFF and the pod was last seen striking rocks, so it tumbles down the face and comes to rest at its foot, which is the seabed the player is standing on when they get out. A settled pod is also a far better painted still than a descending one. THE CONDITION: SINK-COUNTER >= 3 is the pod submerged, DEPTH == 3 is the bottom. No upper bound -- it is not going anywhere -- and it is visible only at the bottom, which is what gives swimming DOWN a reason once the climb has started. THE DOWN CAP VARIANT IS WITHDRAWN AND MUST NOT COME BACK (2026-09-16). The user reported seeing TWO pods on the sea floor, and they were: the two paintings put the pod in different places. Measured by diffing each variant against its own base and unprojecting the centroid through that view's camera, the level view puts the pod at bearing 162.6 and elevation -7.7, and the cap put it at bearing 146.2 and elevation -50.5 -- sixteen degrees apart in bearing, which no single object can be, and elevations implying distances that differ ninefold. The level view is the right one: at elevation -7.7 with the eye 1.6 m up, the pod lies about 11.8 m off. THE CAP CANNOT SEE IT. A 131-degree cap reaches elevation -24.5 on its axes and -17.9 at its corners, so a thing at -7.7 is outside it altogether. Dev's DR-111 request asked for a cap variant that the geometry forbids, and the only way to satisfy it was to paint a second, nearer pod. Looking down in this state correctly shows bare seabed.

notes: Canon: "You have entered a tiny room with a sliding door to the south which is <open/closed>. A control panel contains an Up button, a Down button, and a narrow slot." (compone.zil 2403-2410; DDESC, globals.zil 363-367). Flags RLANDBIT ONBIT, no FLOYDBIT (2399). Globals LIGHTS CONTROLS SLOT ELEVATOR-BUTTON UPPER-ELEVATOR-DOOR (2400). No scenery words. Nothing starts here.

Size is INFERRED. "Tiny" is canon but no number is, and the door is not free: 2.2 x 2.5 is fixed by the Elevator Lobby's and Tower Core's packages, and Tower Core's shell is already cut with that frame. A 2.2 m door needs about 0.8 m of jamb each side, which is why the room is 3.8 m across. The word survives by contrast, which is how the game uses it: this car 12.9 m2, the Reactor car 15.1 ("an elevator", compone.zil 1503), the Lower car 20.2 ("medium-sized", 2434).
SOUTH and OUT are one hole. UP and DOWN are blocked commands with no aperture at all: travel starts only at the buttons.

The same car shell appears at both landings; only what is through the door changes. That is why the two landings are separate CONDITIONS here rather than a line of prose -- turn.js reads the condition off a view's own `state` field and derives nothing from its name, so a variant registered without one is painted, delivered, approved and never shown (the fault of 2026-09-16).

Norm plan (no fabric yet, so no seeds): TURN-000/090/180/270 at pitch 0, HFOV 110, 1672x941, from the eye [0, 1.6, 0]; caps UP/DOWN at bearing 0, pitch +90/-90, their lens from lib/views.mjs ringReach once the fabric exists (131-133 for a four-view 110 ring). audit-turns.mjs against the wall opening above: 4 views x 110 degrees at 0/90/180/270, slack 4.5, offAxis 0. Seam windows 43-47, 133-137, 223-227, 313-317, every one on plain wall. The one opening (bearings 146.1-213.9) is wholly inside TURN-180, 33.9 degrees either side of centre, so TURN-180 carries every landing state and TURN-090 carries the panel. The room's corners are at 48.2 / 131.8 / 228.2 / 311.8, leaving each window 1.2 degrees of clearance on its tight side and 5.2 on the other -- tight, but a 3.8 x 3.4 box has nowhere better.

Beats, not states (ARTWORK-BRIEF 3), no artwork: the wrong-card sign "Inkorekt awtharazaashun kard...akses deeniid" (globals.zil 1435-1436); the scrambled-card sign "Magnetik striip randumiizd..." after carrying the magnet (globals.zil 1379-1381; compone.zil 1595-1610) and this port's re-recorded stripe on a second slide (user decision 2026-09-11 round ten); Floyd producing his own card (globals.zil 1440-1463); the Hawaiian music. If Greg draws the slim sign strip these imply, it is dark in the base.

Dev item for the user, not metadata: TOWER-CORE reaches this car by a direct exit (compone.zil 2733) that checks neither the door nor the car's position, so the player can walk into a car that is not there. It is in the original.

It is in the accepted DR-063 fabric and BOTH neighbours paint it through their doorways -- COMM-ROOM's CORE-PASSAGE beyond says 'the cool ceiling lamp over it' and OBSERVATION-DECK's CORE-DOORWAY 'the cool ceiling lamp over the middle'. Added 2026-09-17: it was in the fabric but not authored here, and an authored fixture list replaces the fabric's lamps outright, so the one lamp the rest of the tower describes was the one lamp not lighting the room.

ELEVATOR-DOORWAY.beyond: UPPER-ELEVATOR, and NOTHING ELSE EVER. The car is the only way into the tower top, it arrives here and stays with its door open, and since 2026-09-17 the exit itself checks that (rules.roomExits['TOWER-CORE|NORTH'] in connectors.js): with the car at the other end of the shaft the door reads closed and the walk is refused, so an empty shaft is never on screen and must never be painted. Open shows the car's interior at its upper stop -- a tiny room 3.8 wide, 3.1 high and 3.4 deep, its far (north) wall 3.4 m beyond the leaf, its cool ceiling lamp at [0, 3.06, 0] in the car's own coordinates, and on its EAST wall at x 1.88 the control panel: the plate at [1.88, 1.35, 0.62], the Up/Down buttons at [1.84, 1.48, 0.62] and the narrow slot at [1.84, 1.05, 0.62] below them. Its own doorway is the same 2.2 x 2.5 hole seen from the other side. Closed shows the plate-steel two-panel leaf, 2.16 x 2.46 at z -3.4 (wwwroot/data/scenes/TOWER-CORE.json), inside the trim frame at [0, 1.25, -3.34], band 0.16, reveal 0.12.
ELEVATOR-DOORWAY.notes: The drum's own gap runs -19 to 19 degrees at radius 3.4 with a 2.5 m head, which is this aperture; the frame is set 0.06 m into it. 2.2 x 2.5 is not free: UPPER-ELEVATOR's package gives its SOUTH mouth the same size, and DR-084 does NOT police that pair, because both of the car's exits are routine exits with target null in world.json. Do not let it drift.

COMM-PASSAGE.beyond: COMM-ROOM, through a short plain passage 0.80 m deep -- the drum is the passage's near end, not the room's wall. Beyond it a small windowless room 6.93 square and 3 m high (compone.zil: "a small room with no windows. The sole exit is southwest"), with a wide console filling either end and thick cables running up into the ceiling. WHAT SHOWS IS LESS THAN IT SOUNDS, and the cone is the reason: the passage's far end is 1.5 m wide at 4.32 m from the eye, which holds every ray inside 9.85 degrees of the axis, so the visible half-width at the Comm Room's far wall 10.8 m off is only 1.88 m. The nearest console stands 2.5 m off the axis and the red "Tranzmishun Reeseevd" lamp 2.96 m, so NEITHER IS IN SIGHT. Paint the reveal, the floor, the far north-east wall and the cable trunk climbing it into the ceiling -- and no console and no blinking lamp. Corrected 2026-09-17: this said the near console end and the LIGHTS fixture showed, which the fabric pass measured and disproved. No door leaf: the game has none here and NORTH is this room's only door.
COMM-PASSAGE.notes: The drum gap runs 32 to 58 degrees at radius 3.4 -- a 1.5 m chord -- with a 2.5 m head. The Comm Room's side of the same passage is 2.4 m high (its CORE-PASSAGE), so the head steps 0.1 m up as you come through; `exits.NE` carries the shared 1.5 x 2.4 that DR-084 compares, this entry's `clear` states the same, and its width and height carry the 2.5 m head that is true on THIS side (the lintel is the 0.1 m wall-panel at the drum's outer face, scripts/fabric-tower.mjs commPassage). One opening, two heights, exactly as the foot and head of a stair are.

DECK-DOORWAY.beyond: OBSERVATION-DECK: straight through the drum's own thickness, no passage. Open air -- the balcony girdling the tower, 14 across and 8 high in its package, its parapet and coping, the sea, the island below and the second island about 20 km east. THIS IS THE ROOM'S ONLY DAYLIGHT AND IT CHANGES WITH THE HOUR: the deck is a sky room lit by the tower's one sun (bearing 235, elevation 35, shared with the Helipad, the Balcony and the Crag), so what stands in this gap is bright and hard at day, orange and low at dusk, and near-black at dark, while the core's own lamps do not change at all. At dusk and dark the deck's package says this doorway is the one warm thing in ITS room; from in here the relation is the other way round, and the gap is a cut-out of a different world.
DECK-DOORWAY.notes: The drum gap runs 212 to 238 degrees at radius 3.4, a 1.5 m chord, head 2.5 -- and that is the whole doorway: the deck's side is the same gap through the drum's 0.12 m, with no lintel (unlike the north-east passage), so `exits.SW` and the deck's NE both state 1.5 x 2.5. notes: A SKY ROOM (SHARED-ROOM-METADATA.json metadata.sky.rooms) and a strange one: it is outdoors half a kilometre up and sees NOTHING but sky. "A fence prevents you from approaching the perimeter, so your view is limited to cloud-filled sky" (compone.zil 2745-2746). No ocean, no island, no complex, no horizon, no tower below -- in any view, any cap, any phase. It still needs all three DAY-PHASE looks, because the sky over it changes all day.
DAY STATES: the three phases and nothing else. No flood variants -- the sea is not visible from here at any hour on any day.

THE FENCE IS WHAT SIZES THE ROOM, and this is the room's one real piece of arithmetic. The eye is 1.6 m up at the centre of the pad; the horizon from 500 m is 0.72 degrees BELOW level, so a fence that hides it must stand above the line from the eye to the horizon, and to hide the island and the sea it must reach higher still. At a radius of 16 m a fence 2.5 m tall blocks everything below 3.2 degrees above the eye, which hides the horizon with 4 degrees to spare and leaves only sky. Wider pad, taller fence: the pair have to be chosen together, and 32 m across with a 2.5 m fence is the pair that also fits the machine. Solid lower panels to about 1.2 m with heavy mesh above, one continuous run, no gate.

WHY THE PAD GREW from v1's 18 m. A craft with a 4.8 by 8.5 m cabin is about 5.6 m across and 14.4 m nose to tail with a 12 m rotor. Parked 10 m from the eye it spans bearings 54 to 126 and sits wholly inside the view facing 90; parked 4.8 m from the eye, as v2 had it, it spans 41 to 118 and lies across the seam at 45, which is two paintings disagreeing about a rotor. The pad has to be wide enough to stand back from the machine. The game agrees: "a wide, flat area", and the fence is far enough off that the player never reaches it.

VIEW PLAN (node scripts/audit-turns.mjs): 4 views x 110 degrees at 0/90/180/270, every seam on plain wall, offAxis 0. 90 is the craft and its open doors, 270 is the stairhead and the shaft, 0 and 180 are plain deck and fence under sky -- the two cheap views that pay for the two that matter. Seams at 45, 135, 225 and 315 fall on empty deck and plain fence. Plus two caps: up is the rotor overhead against cloud, down is the deck's radial plating with the stairhead at its western edge.

FABRIC (for whoever cuts it): parts.js `open`, a 32 m deck disc, a fence ring at radius 16 and 2.5 m high, the `spiral` stair at [-4.4, 0, 0] with its guard ring, and the craft as props -- fuselage, gear, mast, four blades, tail boom and fin. No sea part, no rock, no sky matte below the fence. It is the cheapest fabric of the three outdoor tower rooms because nothing outside the fence exists.

THE CRAFT'S CABIN FLOOR IS 1.6 M ABOVE THE DECK, and that number is shared with HELICOPTER, where it is what makes the game's other sentence true: from inside the craft the eye is 3.2 m above the deck, which is 0.7 m ABOVE this fence, so the windows see the pad and the ocean beyond it while a player standing on the pad sees only sky. The two descriptions only agree if the cabin is up on its gear. Whoever cuts either room must keep the pair: fence top 2.5 m, cabin floor 1.6 m.

SHARED WITH ITS NEIGHBOURS: (1) HELICOPTER -- the same machine, the same open doors, the same rust, and the fence and deck seen back through them; the cabin floor height above. (2) TOWER-CORE -- the same spiral stair, one handedness, the shaft's concrete and its warm lamps at the bottom. (3) OBSERVATION-DECK -- the same tower, far below this deck; the pad's underside and its shaft are in that room's ceiling cap, and this fence is why the pad is not in that room's view of the sky.
Nothing below the fence line appears in any view, and no marking, beacon, second craft, external control or readable lettering is added.

notes: IT IS A ROOM, not an art room, and that is the first question this package has to answer. The Escape Pod's safety web became a second eye on one room because SAFETY-WEB is a VEHBIT object inside ESCAPE-POD and climbing into it does not change where the player is (ESCAPE-POD-WEB, DR-112). This is the opposite case: HELICOPTER is a `<ROOM>` in the source (compone.zil 2792-2807) with its own LDESC, its own globals and its own OUT, and HELICOPTER-OBJECT-F does `<GOTO ,HELICOPTER>` when the player boards (compone.zil 2775-2779). The game moves the player; HERE changes; the status line changes. So it gets what any room gets -- one eye, one ring of four, two caps -- and nothing has to be wired in `viewOf` or `altViews`. The vehicle-ness only shows in the metadata as the IN/OUT pair being exempt from the shared-size rule.

A SKY ROOM (SHARED-ROOM-METADATA.json metadata.sky.rooms) even though the player is indoors: every phase reaches this cabin through three openings, and half of what is on screen in two of the four views is outside. It needs all three DAY-PHASE looks, and they must be the same looks the Helipad uses, because it is the same sky 6 m away.
DAY STATES: the three phases and nothing else. No flood variants; no sea rise is visible from 500 m (see OBSERVATION-DECK's note), and nothing else about this cabin ever changes.

THE CABIN FLOOR IS 1.6 M ABOVE THE PAD DECK, and that single number is what makes the game consistent. From the pad, "your view is limited to cloud-filled sky" -- the fence hides everything. From inside this craft, "through the windows of the vehicle you can see a wide Helipad, and beyond that, endless ocean far below". Both are true only if this eye is above the fence: standing on the cabin floor the eye is 3.2 m over the deck, 0.7 m above the 2.5 m fence, so every opening looks down over it to the sea. Drop the cabin to the deck and the room's own description becomes false. Whoever cuts either room keeps the pair: fence 2.5 m, cabin floor 1.6 m.

ORIENTATION: the craft's nose is north, matching the way it is parked on the pad, so this room's compass is the world's. Forward is 0, the way out is 270, the ocean view is 90, the aft bulkhead is 180.

VIEW PLAN (node scripts/audit-turns.mjs): 4 views x 110 degrees at 0/90/180/270, every seam on plain wall, offAxis 0. 0 is the forward bulkhead, the cover, the lock and the windows; 270 is the open west doors and the pad; 90 is the east door and the ocean; 180 is the empty bay and the plain aft bulkhead. Seams at 45, 135, 225 and 315 fall on plain rusted flank and on the cabin's four corners. Plus two caps: up is the ribbed roof, down is the tie-down plating. NO FURTHER APERTURE MAY BE CUT within about 20 degrees of a seam -- that rules out portholes along the flanks fore and aft, which is why the several doors are gathered amidships rather than spread down the side.

FABRIC (for whoever cuts it): a `shell` 4.8 x 2.8 x 8.5 with openings WEST, EAST and NORTH as stated, ribs and tie-down plating as props, the control mass and its cover on the forward bulkhead, and the two folded-back leaves. Everything outside is HELIPAD's fabric seen through the openings -- deck, fence, sky, sea -- so the two rooms must be cut from ONE layout, as the Kalamontee rooms are (fabric-kalamontee.mjs), with this cabin's origin at [10.0, 1.6, 0] in the pad's frame.

SHARED WITH HELIPAD, and both must agree: the machine's outside (5.6 m across, 14.4 m nose to tail, four blades set fore, aft, port and starboard), the west doors' size and sill, the rust, the fence's height and distance in each direction (26 m west, 16 m north and south, 6 m east) and the sun. A view out of this cabin and a view of this cabin are the same place.
Nothing in here is takeable, nothing is stored in the bay, the cover never opens, the doors never close and the craft never flies: "The controls seem to be locked."

notes: A SKY ROOM (SHARED-ROOM-METADATA.json metadata.sky.rooms), and the one with the most sky in it: the eye is half a kilometre up with 270 degrees of open air round it. It needs all three DAY-PHASE looks and it needs them to agree with the status line, because the player can stand here at any hour.

DAY STATES: the three phases and NOTHING ELSE. No flood variants, and that is a decision with a reason. The sea rises one room a day in the ruins (WATER-LEVEL-F, compone.zil 151-160; rules/ship.js 293-308), and BALCONY, CRAG, WINDING-STAIR and COURTYARD carry painted day states for it. This room is different on three counts: the game never changes its description by day; both islands are ringed by cliffs seen from over the top (the approach painted for ESCAPE-POD-WEB, state ISLANDS-3000), so a rise of tens of metres moves the surf line by a few metres against a shoreline kilometres long; and the eye is 500 m above it, where that is well under a pixel. If the user wants the flood to show here anyway, it is cheap -- only the views that contain the shore change -- but it should be asked for, not assumed.

GEOMETRY, and what is inferred. The game says only: a balcony girdling the tower, the tower about half a kilometre tall, the island below with the complex sprawling directly beneath and the dormitory section on the far side, a second island about 20 km east, and one doorway north-east (compone.zil 3134-3150). Everything else here is dev's inference, but it is not free invention: the doorway's position in v1 and the Tower Core's drum agree exactly, and that fixes the plan. The core's axis is 9.27 m north-east of the eye, at [6.55, -6.55]; its drum, radius 3.4 and 4.2 m high, is this room's inner wall. The terrace floor runs from that drum out to a parapet on an arc of radius 11.5 m about the same axis, which passes 2.23 m south-west of the eye at [-1.58, 1.58]. The parapet is 1.1 m of solid coping with a pipe rail to 1.35 m. The terrace is the crown's open south-west quadrant, about 8 m deep; north-west and south-east of it the crown's enclosed mass (the Comm Room and the Upper Elevator) comes out to about 9.8 m and the walkway narrows to a metre or two and carries on round the tower, which is how it girdles it without being a ring the player can walk.

THE ROOM IS NOT ROOFED BY ITS OWN ENVELOPE, BUT IT IS OVERHUNG. The envelope's 8 m is the crown wall rising behind the eye, not a ceiling; the v1 envelope of [12, 3.2, 12] read as a 3.2 m soffit over the terrace and is withdrawn. What IS overhead is the Helipad. Corrected 2026-09-17 (the user's decision, after the tower fabric was cut): this said the ceiling cap is sky with the pad glimpsed far above on a narrower shaft, and that is not what the geometry gives. The pad is 32 m across against the crown's 11.5 m parapet, so its deck overhangs the whole terrace. MEASURED ON THE CUT SCENE, from this room's own eye: straight up is the pad's underside at 28.2 m, and it is still the pad's underside at 89 degrees on every bearing. Sky appears only lower down and only to the south and west -- first reached at about 64 degrees on bearing 135, 71 on 180, 70 on 225, 75 on 270 and 70 on 315 -- and NEVER to the north, north-east or east down to 20 degrees, where the drum, the crown wall and the Comm Room's mass stand. So the up cap is a lopsided field of concrete soffit around the zenith with a crescent of sky off the seaward side, not a sky cap. The room's daylight arrives SIDEWAYS over the parapet, not from above, which is what makes the sun's 35-degree elevation on bearing 235 do the work here.

VIEW PLAN (node scripts/audit-turns.mjs): 4 views x 110 degrees at 45/135/225/315, every seam on plain wall, offAxis 0 -- the same set v1's exit table gave. 45 is the doorway and the drum; 225 is the open sea over the parapet with the sun in it; 135 and 315 run along the terrace each way with the island under the rail. Seams at 0, 90, 180 and 270 fall on plain coping and plain drum. Plus two caps: up is sky and the crown wall, down is the terrace's own flags with the coping and a sliver of the drop at its edge.

FABRIC (for whoever cuts it): parts.js `open`, then a `drum` of radius 3.4 at [6.55, 0, -6.55] with a gap for the doorway, a terrace floor and a parapet ring about the same axis, the crown's flanking masses as props, a `sea` at level -500, and ONE low-detail rock mass for the island's plateau. The complex 500 m below is PAINTED, not modelled -- there is no way to model an abandoned campus as a blockout and no need to. Set the sea part's radius to at least 40 km: the camera's far plane is 40 km (DR-109), so a disc at least that big is clipped by the far plane and its horizon sits 0.72 degrees below level, which is the true horizon dip from 500 m; the kit's default 30 km disc would end 0.24 degrees low and give the painter a false horizon.

SHARED WITH ITS NEIGHBOURS, and both must agree: (1) TOWER-CORE -- its drum is this room's inner wall and its south-west gap is this room's doorway; the two packages agree on 1.5 x 2.4 today, and the core's 2.5 m head against this room's 2.4 is a step in the reveal, not a disagreement. (2) COMM-ROOM -- it is the crown's north-east mass, which is what puts the parapet at 11.5 m and narrows the walkway on that side. (3) HELIPAD -- it is the top of the same tower, well above this room on a narrower shaft; the pad's underside and that shaft are what the player sees in this room's ceiling cap, and this room is what the Helipad's fence hides.

The parapet is safety geometry, not an exit: the game gives one route out, and the only thing over the rail is OCEAN, which answers "You can't reach the ocean from here" (OCEAN-F, globals.zil 167-171). The deck has no CLIFF global and nothing can be thrown off it. No aircraft, no pad equipment and no second doorway appears in any view.

ENUNCIATOR-PSEUDO.label: enunciator
ENUNCIATOR-PSEUDO.notes: Seven lamps in red, blue, green, yellow, gray, brown and pink (canon's black, made pink by the user 2026-09-23), in that order (compone.zil 2854-2869). The panel is PAINTED ONCE WITH EVERY LAMP DARK; the lamp that flashes is an engine OVERLAY over the painting (`overlays` ENUNCIATOR-LAMP-1-RED to -7-PINK, each a `cutout` on its own CHEMICAL-REQUIRED value), not seven paintings of one panel, and not a fabric box either. Flat and additive is an overlay, per ARTWORK-BRIEF section 3. Seven overlays and not one panel of seven lamps: a `when` belongs to a part, never to a lamp inside one (scene/design.js overlayPart lifts only the part-level `condition`), and a `panel` part is not one of the kinds that may stand in front of a painting (dashboard/uat.js) nor one the schema allows as an overlay. Done 2026-09-22 (Norm); before it the seven lamps were `prop` boxes 10 cm deep in the room’s fabric (scripts/fabric-tower.mjs), which stood 1.2 cm left of the painted lenses and read 8 px wide against their 5. The schema allows no labelOffset on a pseudo, so its plate keeps the default height; if it lies on the lamps it wants the panel moved or the schema widened (Norm, 2026-09-22).

It carries no states.DAY-PHASE and needs none: its light is the same at noon and at midnight, so it authors fixtures instead (DR-092). THE ROOM IS TURNED 45 DEGREES, and that is the whole geometry decision. A regular octagon, apothem 3.2 m (6.4 m across the flats, 6.93 m across the corners), 3.0 m high, its walls centred on bearings 0, 45, 90 ... 315. The receive console fills the north-west wall (315), the send console the south-east wall (135), the doorway is centred in the south-west wall (225) and the cable trunk climbs the north-east wall (45). Why: the game gives one exit, south-west, and two consoles at opposite ends whose signs and lamps change state. On a compass-aligned box the consoles sit at 90 and 270 and the door at 225, and no four-view ring can put a view on all three -- the recorded plan for v1 (45.9/135.9/225.9/315.9) puts a SEAM down the middle of each console, which is the one thing the port has learned not to do with a thing that changes. Turned onto the tower's own axis, the four views land on the doorway and on each console and on the cables, and the four seams (0/90/180/270) fall on the four plain narrow walls between them. The tower is already built on this axis: TOWER-CORE's two passages are gaps at 32-58 and 212-238 degrees in its drum.

VIEW PLAN (node scripts/audit-turns.mjs, after this revision): 4 views x 110 degrees at 45/135/225/315, every seam on plain wall, offAxis 0. Before this revision the same tool returned 4 x 110 at 45.9/135.9/225.9/315.9 from the old door position; the set is the same four views a degree round, but on the old geometry it faced a door and two walls instead of a door and two consoles. Plus the two caps: ceiling (cable trunking and the two light strips) and floor (plain worn plate).

FABRIC (for whoever cuts it): parts.js `prism`, sides 8, apothem 3.2, height 3.0, first 0, openings { "225": [0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.4] }, floor concrete-worn, wall wall-panel, ceiling ceiling. Then the two console masses as props against the 315 and 135 faces (about 2.4 x 1.1 x 0.7 each), the cable trunk against the 45 face, and the two ceiling strips. Nothing else: the room has no furniture, no chair and no second door.

WHERE IT SITS IN THE TOWER (inferred, shared with OBSERVATION-DECK and HELIPAD): the tower's crown at this level is a drum about 11.5 m in radius. The Tower Core drum (radius 3.4) stands in it; this room is packed against the core's north-east side, its own centre about 7.6 m north-east of the core's axis, so its far corner reaches about 11 m -- which is what sets the crown's radius, and therefore where the Observation Deck's parapet runs. The room's outer walls are buried in the crown, which is why it has no windows.
The consoles' lettering is quoted exactly and never modernised: "Reeseev Staashun", "Tranzmishun Reeseevd", "Mesij Plaabak", "Send Staashun", "Kuulint Sistum Manyuuwul Oovuriid".
Nothing in this room is an exit but the south-west doorway, and no console element is takeable or movable.

LOWER-ELEVATOR-MOUTH.beyond: TWO landings through one hole, by LOWER-ELEVATOR-UP; the car never turns, so both are straight out of the north wall. The aperture is 3.4 m wide at 2.04 m from the eye, so the cone through it is 39.8 degrees off north and the visible half-width at distance d is 0.833 d -- a notably wider window on the world than the Upper car's. (1) LOWER-ELEVATOR-UP == true -- ELEVATOR-LOBBY, cut at 12 x 3.8 x 10 with this hole in its south wall (fabric-kalamontee.mjs 108-110): its deck running 12.2 m north, its far north wall over its whole 12 m width and full height, the 2.2 x 2.5 BLUE DOOR in that wall at bearings 354.9-5.1 with the blue button 1.55 m east of its centre at 7.3, and the lobby's side walls from lobby z 0 northward. The Corridor Junction mouth west and the Booth 2 mouth east fall at bearings 320.2 and 39.8, which is exactly the jamb line (the lobby is 12 m wide and this eye stands 7.2 m from its middle): treat them as NOT seen, and fix that deliberately, because a few centimetres of wall thickness would flip it. The blue door's own state shows -- see states.LOBBY-BLUE-OPEN. (2) LOWER-ELEVATOR-UP != true -- WAITING-AREA, a concrete platform (compone.zil 3155-3158) at 12 x 4.0 x 8: its far north wall 10.2 m off over its whole width and height, and the BENCHES along that wall, which are the thing the doorway frames. Of its east continuation only a sliver is seen: the Kalamontee mouth is 4.0 m wide in the east wall running z -2.0 to +2.0 and the jamb cuts it at z -0.88, so 1.12 m of its north end shows at bearings 35.7-39.8, hard against the frame edge. Paint that sliver, not the whole mouth. No sky at either landing. Derive both glimpses from the neighbours' own packages.
LOWER-ELEVATOR-MOUTH.notes: NORTH and OUT are this one hole (compone.zil 2421-2423, both PER ELEVATOR-EXIT-F; rules.exitDoors.ELEVATOR-EXIT-F resolves both to LOWER-ELEVATOR-DOOR). 3.4 x 3.0 is fixed by ELEVATOR-LOBBY exits.SOUTH (cut in fabric-kalamontee.mjs 110, with a shut leaf at [0, 1.5, 5.08]) and by WAITING-AREA exits.SOUTH/IN. check_design.mjs DR-084 does NOT police any of it: every exit involved is a routine exit with target null. Both landings are on the car's NORTH side, as both of the Upper car's are on its south -- the lobby's red door is in the lobby's own south wall (compone.zil 2368-2369, 2583) and the Waiting Area's metal door in its south wall (3157-3158), so the car hangs below the lobby and above the platform on one axis.

NORTH.notes: The car's one opening. It reaches ELEVATOR-LOBBY when LOWER-ELEVATOR-UP is true and WAITING-AREA when false (compone.zil 2467-2476); shut, it answers "The door is closed."

OUT.notes: Parser alias for NORTH; one physical opening, and graybox folds it into the NORTH panel. Do not build a second hole.

UP.notes: Blocked: prints "You'll have to use the elevator controls." (compone.zil 2425). No hatch, no shaft opening, nothing to draw and nothing to click; no position, so no proxy.

DOWN.notes: Blocked: prints "You'll have to use the elevator controls." (compone.zil 2426). No hatch, no shaft opening, nothing to draw and nothing to click; no position, so no proxy.

LOWER-ELEVATOR-DOOR.notes: The red metal door (compone.zil 2497-2503), NDESCBIT DOORBIT, starting shut. It operates itself: from either landing it reads as already-open only while the car is at that landing, and otherwise "It won't budge." / "You can't close it yourself." (2505-2528). It closes when a trip starts (2614, 2633) and opens on arrival (2693, 2699) or when the red button's summons lands (2578). The lobby is told about it before it moves: "The red door begins vibrating a bit." (2565).

notes: Canon in full (CONTROL-CABIN-F, globals.zil:1687-1700): a small control cabin; a control panel containing a slot, a lever and a display; the lever settable central, up to a position labelled + or down to one labelled -; the display a digital readout showing the velocity; and the cabin window.

NO SEAT. Canon never furnishes this cabin, and the crash text has the operator 'thrown forward into the control panel', which is a standing station. The package's operator chair had no source and has been taken out of the metadata rather than left for a painter to believe.
The console carries exactly three things and they sit in canon's order left to right from the operator: slot, lever, display.

Norm plan: TURN-000/090/180/270, pitch 0, HFOV 110, 1672x941; caps bearing 0, pitch +90/-90, HFOV 131, 1254 square. The window is at bearing 90 and the door at 270, each wholly inside one view, and every seam (45/135/225/315) lands on a plain side wall. Confirmed against planRing with the wallOpenings above.
Cost of the states: every window state is one repaint of TURN-090 and every door state one repaint of TURN-270. The two side views and both caps are untouched by everything this room does.

Envelope raised from the package's 4.4 x 3.0 x 3.2, which made the cabin longer than it was wide and narrower than the hull it sits in. This cabin is the east end of the same vehicle as SHUTTLE-CAR-ALFIE, so it has the car's 4.8 m beam; 2.8 m fore-and-aft is the least that fits console, operator and door sweep, and is what makes 'small' true. All three numbers are inferred: canon states no dimension.

LEVER-UP.notes: The lever at its upper (+) position, drawn over the painted one at the central detent: a patch of TURN-090 cut and redrawn by scripts/shuttle-overlays.mjs (LEVER-F, globals.zil 1861-1899). Up and down, as canon has it (the painting puts its + and - marks either side of the boss).

LEVER-DOWN.notes: The lever at its lower (-) position, as LEVER-UP.

DISPLAY.notes: The display reads SHUTTLE-VELOCITY while the car is between stations, and blinks while the lever is off centre (DESCRIBE-SHUTTLE-TRIP: "The display blinks, and now reads ..."). Its face is the painting's with the painted 0 taken out; the digits are the painting's own 5 x 7 dot matrix. At a station it is the painted 0.

TUNNEL-MOTION.notes: The tunnel going by in the forward window, over the painted bore: wall lamps streaking past, panel joints and rail glints, at SHUTTLE-VELOCITY x 0.5 m/s and still when the car has stopped between stations. At SHUTTLE-COUNTER 23 a glow at the vanishing point: "The shuttle car is approaching a brightly-lit area" (DESCRIBE-SHUTTLE-TRIP). Only the cabin whose window looks down the bore -- the one that started the car. Drawn by the engine (scene/parts.js tunnel); the tunnel's section is scripts/fabric-shuttle.mjs's.

EAST.notes: The room's only exit, and only while SHUTTLE-DOOR is open (globals.zil:1612). One hole with SHUTTLE-CAR-ALFIE's WEST door.

CABIN-DOOR.beyond: SHUTTLE-CAR-ALFIE, end-on down its whole 12 m: fixed seating along both long walls, the clear freight deck, and off the centreline to the left at about 6 m the north platform doorway with cooler, greyer platform concrete showing through it. The far bulkhead carries the matching east door to ALFIE-CONTROL-EAST, open or shut as this one is. While SHUTTLE-MOVING a closed sliding leaf fills this opening and none of the car is visible.
CABIN-DOOR.notes: Sill on the deck. At a station SHUTTLE-DOOR carries OPENBIT and INVISIBLE (globals.zil:1628), so no leaf is painted in the base.

FORWARD-WINDOW.beyond: Whatever DESCRIBE-VIEW says (globals.zil:1702-1718), and nothing else. At Kalamontee, which is where the game starts: a featureless concrete wall, close -- the buffer at the west end of the station. At Lawanda: twin rails on the floor of a long tunnel running away west and vanishing. While SHUTTLE-MOVING with SHUTTLE-COUNTER 23: those rails ending at a brightly lit station ahead.
FORWARD-WINDOW.notes: Centre dropped from the package's y 2.02 to y 1.80, sill 1.35, head 2.25. At 2.02 the sill stood at 1.57, above the eye at 1.6, and canon requires the operator to see rails running along the FLOOR of the tunnel; a sill above eye height cannot show a floor. At 1.35 the sill is 0.25 m below the eye and 1.38 m from it, so the sightline falls 0.181 per metre: the tunnel floor comes into view about 14.3 m ahead (the rail tops about 13.8) and runs off to the vanishing point. Corrected 2026-09-17: it read about nine metres, which is the answer for a tunnel floor level with the cabin deck (1.6 / 0.181 = 8.8). The accepted Lawanda berth puts the track bed 1.0 m down, so the drop is 2.6 m and not 1.6, and the sill still clears the console top at 1.26. Width is inferred -- the console's width and a little, in a 4.8 m wall. It does not open (globals.zil:126).

SLOT.label: slot
SLOT.notes: Canon (globals.zil:1366-1372): about ten centimetres wide, only about two centimetres deep, parallel ridges of metal down its long sides. Shallow -- a card is slid through it. To the operator's left of the lever, which mirrors to the far side of the cabin in room coordinates.

LEVER.label: lever
LEVER.notes: Three settings, LEVER-SETTING 1 / 0 / -1: upper, central, lower (globals.zil:1861-1899). Only those two marks on the track. Painted at the central detent in the base.

WINDOW.label: window
WINDOW.notes: The cabin window of the room description. Its pick proxy sits in the FORWARD-WINDOW aperture; what is seen through it follows DESCRIBE-VIEW.

GLOBAL-SHUTTLE.label: shuttle car
GLOBAL-SHUTTLE.notes: Cabin-shell vocabulary. ENTER here answers 'You ARE in the shuttle car'; EXIT answers that you cannot leave the car from here (globals.zil:1567-1574). Proxy clear of the east doorway and the console.

SHUTTLE-DISPLAY-PSEUDO.label: display
SHUTTLE-DISPLAY-PSEUDO.notes: The digital readout, to the operator's right. Never dark: the room description reads it out whether or not the car is live (rules/connectors.js:516, DR-083). Reads SHUTTLE-VELOCITY; 0 in the base.

LEVER-POSITION-PSEUDO.label: lever position
LEVER-POSITION-PSEUDO.notes: The lever's three positions as a thing the player can name -- CENTER, CENTRE, CENTRAL, MIDDLE, POSITION (rules/connectors.js:497). The proxy is the marked plate on the console skirt directly below the lever's travel, so the lever and its positions stay separately clickable and no two pick boxes in this small console intersect. Added because check_design reported the room had this scenery routine and the package did not describe it.

constraints: keep the east doorway lane, the console face and the dropped-item anchors clear
FLOYD.notes: Floyd follows into this room without comment (compone.zil:2221-2228).

SHUTTLE-DOOR.notes: One game door drives this face, the east cabin's and both ends of the car; they open and shut together. Open and INVISIBLE at a station, so no leaf is painted in the base.

droppedItems.notes: Four corner anchors inside a small cabin, clear of the east door lane, the console face and conditional Floyd.

lighting.notes: Lit cabin (ONBIT): even interior light with the console's own glow, no sun, no sky, no day phase. In the base state the forward window admits nothing at all -- it looks at a concrete wall a couple of metres off -- so the window is the dullest surface in the room, not the brightest.

BETWEEN-STATIONS.notes: Between stations the car runs on its own lamps, with no platform light coming in: the paintings about a tenth darker while SHUTTLE-MOVING (scripts/shuttle-overlays.mjs). On states.BETWEEN-STATIONS rather than on MOVING, because the light is the same in both cabins whichever way the car is running.

The car is the same vehicle: envelope 12 x 3.4 x 4.8, eye at the middle, both 1.5 x 2.4 end doorways and the 2.6 x 2.5 platform doorway are SHUTTLE-CAR-ALFIE v2's numbers (RoomPolishInstructions/SHUTTLE-CAR-ALFIE_Visual-Design-Handoff/SHUTTLE-CAR-ALFIE/SHUTTLE-CAR-ALFIE.metadata.json). Her ends are not swapped -- the east cabin is still east (globals.zil:1651-1652). Nothing takeable is painted into the freight space.
The passenger cabin has no window. WINDOW is a local global of the control cabins only (globals.zil:1666, 1678).
No lettering. Canon gives the car no name board or sign; 'Shuttle Car Betty' is the room's DESC, not something written on it.

HOW TO MEASURE THIS RIM, AND WHAT A PLAYER ACTUALLY SEES -- these are two different rules and the entry used to give only the first, stated as though it were both. AT BUILD TIME: reproject gives each direction to whichever view sees it most centrally, so only ONE view's rim goes into the comp at any bearing -- TURN-345 over bearings 0-91 and 293-359, TURN-DOWN over 92-152, TURN-252 over 153-292 (bearings taken round the table from its centre, 0 = north). A measurement must therefore read the owning view and must NOT average the views that frame a bearing; that part was hard-won and it stands. The heart-shaped notch the user photographed on 2026-09-15 lived almost entirely in the arc this cap owns, which is why fixing the cap mattered far more than its area suggests -- and why TURN-345's shortfall at bearings 93-106 and TURN-252's at 143-152 never show in a comp, except inside the cross-fade band. AT RUNTIME it is the other way round: the ring is drawn OVER the cap. wwwroot/scene/parts.js sets mesh.renderOrder = (depth ? -1 : 10) - (cap ? 1 : 0), with the comment "a cap is built from the level views and its rim is theirs twice resampled, so it goes underneath: the ring shows wherever it reaches, and the cap wherever the ring fades out above or below it". So what a player sees at a given bearing is the RING's rim wherever the ring reaches, and the cap only below the ring's bottom feather. An earlier version of this note claimed the build-time ownership held at runtime too; it does not. THE CONSEQUENCE, which is the useful part: a steep downward view shows the cap in the middle with a ring view to either side, so every disagreement between neighbours lands on a boundary INSIDE that one frame -- which is why two defects show up roughly symmetric about the centre of such a shot, and why agreement between neighbouring views can matter more to the eye than accuracy in any one of them. And one arc is never enough on its own -- the eye is south-east of the table, so this cap frames only 74-169 of the rim, and an even arc there says nothing about the rest.

CREVICE.notes: "a jagged crevice crosses the floor" (compone.zil 924); the CREVICE object, NDESCBIT and fixed (944-950), EXAMINE/SEARCH through CREVICE-F (952-962; rules/connectors.js 179-193). The box is also the floor's pick target here: GROUND has this room's own EXAMINE, SEARCH and LOOK UNDER answer (globals.zil 71-73; rules/connectors.js 166-177), and a floor cannot carry a wall plaque, so the crevice it describes stands in for it (accepted by Norm, the fix pass, 14 Sep). The user, 2026-09-16: "text for 'crevice' overlays the key - makes it hard to see the key". A LARGE OBJECT IS ONLY THE PAINTING’S IN THE STATE THE PAINTING SHOWS IT. largeObjects suppresses an object’s graybox box so it cannot stand in front of the picture that already draws it -- but until 2026-09-17 it did so unconditionally, so an object the room paints in ONE state was invisible in all the others. This room is the case that found it: the ladder is painted across the rift and nothing else, yet it can be dropped or extended on this floor, where nothing draws it at all. `largeObjects.<id>.paintedWhen` now names the state, and an object without one is still the painting’s in every view (wwwroot/scene/design.js, wwwroot/scene/graybox.js). Worth checking wherever a package lists a large object that moves: a fixture like the escape pod’s safety web wants no condition, a thing the player can carry almost certainly does.

Every one of the twelve overlaps between 0.993 and 1.006, all four level views measuring exactly 120 as hung at sharpness 9.3 to 12.4, seam disagreements 0.9, 1, 2.4 and 2.8. That join falls within a few pixels of the Systems Monitors doorway jamb, so the detector reads the jamb -- lit wall against shadowed reveal -- as a step between paintings. The two paintings themselves agree exactly: their overlap measures 1.000. This is the same class as ADMIN-CORRIDOR-N, where the same detector found a riveted panel joint beside the join, and as TURN-263's own join, which falls at a doorway. HOW IT WAS JUDGED, because the numbers and the picture disagreed and the picture won. A strip-sampling profile down the join reported the new part 2 to 24 points darker and 8 to 28 points more saturated at every height, and restore reports a STEP on this join at rows 160-279. A 40 px sampling strip either side of the join straddles that joint and reads its contrast as a seam. So: do not run a strip profile across this join, and do not send these views back on that step. Look at the boundary instead. The same caution applies to ADMIN-CORRIDOR TURN-263, for a different reason (its join falls at a doorway).

R1 was sent back for painting the new middle as smooth cold blockout grey (saturation 4% where the seeds carry 20-34%); R2 overshot into heavy rust. R3 is right. HOW IT WAS JUDGED, because the numbers and the picture disagreed and the picture won. A strip-sampling profile down the join reported the new part 2 to 24 points darker and 8 to 28 points more saturated at every height, and restore reports a STEP on this join at rows 160-279. Neither is a seam. Magnified five times with the join column ticked, the texture, the rust streaking, the horizontal panel line and the eye-height band all run straight across the boundary with no discontinuity at all. What both instruments found is the RIVETED PANEL JOINT about 26 px to the side of the join -- a real feature of the wall, which restore even names by its x. A 40 px sampling strip either side of the join straddles that joint and reads its contrast as a seam. So: do not run a strip profile across this join, and do not send these views back on that step. Look at the boundary instead. The same caution applies to ADMIN-CORRIDOR TURN-263, for a different reason (its join falls at a doorway).

East at x 983 and west at x 270 are in the fabric too -- the walls meeting the ceiling. The south one at y 983 is not in the fabric and was looked at rather than guessed: magnified five times with the join ticked, it is a CEILING LAMP lying across the boundary, its glow against dark ribbed ceiling. The fabric draws that fixture as a flat emissive panel, so its edge does not line up closely enough for the check to match them. Do not seam-edit it; it is the lamp.

The reason: no ring puts every seam window on bare wall. The bare stretches, 6 degrees clear of corners, the opening and the fittings, are 321-30, 120-129, 141-158, 234-247 and 293-309. Every ring of 4, 5 or 6 views at integer bearings was searched at lens 100, 110, 115 and 120, with the windows as turn.js solveSeams computes them, and none fits.
